item.title: NVIDIA NeMo Gym Boosts Reliability of Siemens Fuse AI Agent for Standard-Cell Characterization
item.description:
NVIDIA NeMo Gym Boosts Reliability of Siemens Fuse AI Agent for Standard-Cell Characterization

NVIDIA’s open‑source NeMo Gym was used to evaluate and improve the reliability of the Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent that drives the Solido Characterization Suite for standard‑cell characterization.

🔍 Overview

  • AI agents can give remarkable productivity gains in complex chip design workflows, but their tendency to generate plausible yet incorrect artifacts makes reliability a major barrier to production adoption.
  • In multistage engineering workflows, an undetected error early in setup can silently propagate through downstream stages and final artifact generation.
  • Standard‑cell characterization is the process of generating accurate timing, power, and noise models for logic cells across operating conditions and is required whenever a semiconductor foundry issues a new process design kit (PDK).

🛠️ How NeMo Gym Works

  • NeMo Gym is an open library for evaluating and improving models and agents using environments.
  • The NeMo Gym agentic evaluation environment is designed to diagnose failure modes and track error propagation across complex, multistage workflows.
  • It defines the task, tools, state, and a domain‑specific verifier that inspects final outputs (e.g., Liberty .lib files) against verified reference artifacts.
  • Each rollout starts from a clean state, records thinking traces, input and output messages, and tool actions, enabling engineers to trace complete rollout trajectories and identify root causes behind subtle errors.

📊 Evaluation of the Siemens Fuse AI Agent

  • The Siemens Fuse team used NeMo Gym to scale up evaluations of the Solido Characterization Suite agent when calling characterization tools.
  • The agent orchestrates tools from the broader Solido Characterization Suite through the Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent, which exposes Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills to common coding harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
  • Evaluations verified the generated Liberty files against known references, surfacing both common and rare failures such as missing cells, missing corners, incorrect slew thresholds, and timing or power values outside tolerance.
  • Findings guided changes to the agent’s skill and MCP tool descriptions.
  • The measured benchmark composite score increased from approximately 55 % to about 95 % across a benchmark of representative standard‑cell characterization tasks, while turns and output tokens were reduced.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Reliable AI agents can automate the full characterization flow: tool setup, large‑scale SPICE simulation, distributed compute, Liberty file generation, debugging, and final validation.
  • Early‑stage errors that previously propagated silently are now caught by a rigorous verification protocol.
  • Faster, trustworthy automation shortens the time required to regenerate and validate timing and power models whenever a foundry updates a PDK.

#AIagents #EDA #NVIDIA #ChipDesign

Source: Optimizing Agent Reliability and Tool Calling Efficiency for Chip Design Using NVIDIA NeMo Gym | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: New Memory Management Frameworks for Long Horizon AI Agents
item.description:
New Memory Management Frameworks for Long Horizon AI Agents

Recent developments in AI agent research introduce new methods for managing interaction history to reduce computational costs while maintaining task performance in long-horizon scenarios.

🔍 Overview

Long-horizon language model agents accumulate interaction history that increases computational costs and makes relevant information harder to reuse. Researchers have found that the need for memory compression and recall is already encoded in the model’s internal representations in the hidden state immediately before an action.

🧩 How it works

Several frameworks have been proposed to optimize how agents handle historical data:

Framework Function Key Mechanism
PaMER Combines state guided compression with external evidence retrieval Uses internal signals to trigger memory operations
PaMER+ Recovering specific historical information Introduces step level evidence selection
StateComp Determines when interactions can be safely compressed Uses a two-stage annotation procedure for KEEP and READY supervision and an imbalance-aware router
ChipMEM Verification-grounded memory for EDA agents Combines cross-task procedural memory with within-trajectory statistical guidance

⚙️ Key details

  • StateComp Implementation: Uses a bounded state representation to reduce the cost of evaluating long histories; adjacent READY interactions are grouped into spans and replaced with summaries.
  • ChipMEM Components:
    • A procedural component that stores skills only after they pass synthesis, simulation, or formal checks.
    • A Bayesian component that maintains hierarchical Beta estimates over tool-call outcomes to rank recovery strategies.
    • A common adapter for RTL optimization and testbench-generation agents.

💡 Why it matters

Experiments on WorkBuddyBench indicate that the PaMER framework substantially reduces context consumption. Specifically, StateComp reduced total agent and summarization tokens by 52.27% and achieved a 12.67-fold speedup in representation extraction while maintaining performance.

On RTLRewriter-Bench, ChipMEM produced equivalence-passing outputs on 39/54 scored designs compared to 35/54 without memory, with mean area improvement increasing from 5.66% to 8.69%. On held-out CVDP tasks, ChipMEM with a frozen procedural library achieved 20/20 accepted outcomes versus 18/20 without memory.

#AIagents #LanguageModels #MemoryManagement #EDA

Source: Memory Control Signals Emerge Before Action in Long Horizon Agents Source: StateComp: Learning When to Compress History in Long Horizon Agents Source: ChipMEM: Verification-Grounded Memory for EDA Agents
